title: 2 Samuel 24:10–14
context: David’s conscience strikes him after the census, and he confesses that he has sinned greatly and asks the LORD to take away his iniquity. The prophet Gad brings God’s offer of three judgments, famine, flight before enemies, or pestilence, and David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand because his mercies are great. Both traditions read this as shared ground on repentance and trust in God’s mercy even under judgment.

verses.text: David’s heart struck him after he had counted the people. David said to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in that which I have done. But now, the LORD, put away, I beg you, the iniquity of your servant; for I have done very foolishly.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“David’s heart struck him,” and he confesses, “I have sinned greatly.” Arminian readers note the genuine repentance that follows conviction.

David takes responsibility and asks for forgiveness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see conviction of sin as a work of God’s grace in David’s heart.

Both traditions agree that David is responsible and that confession is the right response (cf. Ps 32:5).

verses.text: When David rose up in the morning, the LORD’s word came to the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
In the morning the LORD’s word comes to Gad, David’s seer. Arminian readers note that God answers David’s confession through a prophet.

Gad had served David since his fugitive years (1 Sam 22:5).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word guiding even the response to David’s sin, coming through the prophet Gad.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the prophet speaks for God, not for himself.

verses.text: “Go and speak to David, ‘The LORD says, “I offer you three things. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
God offers David three choices. Arminian readers note that God involves David in the choice of consequence, treating him as a responsible agent.

The offer shows both justice and mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God setting the terms of judgment while still giving David a real choice among them.

Both traditions agree the choice is genuine and that it takes place within God’s appointed options.

verses.text: So Gad came to David, and told him, saying, “Shall seven years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days’ pestilence in your land? Now answer, and consider what answer I shall return to him who sent me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Gad offers seven years of famine, three months of flight, or three days of pestilence. Arminian readers note that 1 Chronicles 21:12 has three years of famine.

The number difference is a textual issue.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the variant between seven years here and three years in 1 Chronicles 21:12.

Each option is serious, and David must answer the God who sent the prophet; the number difference is left unresolved.

verses.text: David said to Gad, “I am in distress. Let us fall now into the LORD’s hand, for his mercies are great. Let me not fall into man’s hand.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “Let us fall now into the LORD’s hand, for his mercies are great.” Arminian readers note David’s trust in God’s mercy over human cruelty.

He chooses to place himself in God’s hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faith that God’s mercy is greater than man’s (cf. Ps 103:8–14).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground on trusting God’s character.
